title: Suspected Meningitis: Community Recognition and Pre-Hospital Antibiotics

evidenceAudit.scope: Community or pre-hospital recognition of suspected meningitis or meningococcal disease, immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone when transfer is delayed, and urgent hospital transfer.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: NICE NG240 gives no numeric pre-hospital doses; doses are from the NHS Dumfries and Galloway primary care handbook, which links to the British National Formulary for Children for ceftriaxone and cefotaxime paediatric doses.
The ceftriaxone paediatric dose is not given in the sources opened.
No Saudi pre-hospital protocol was opened; emergency medical services protocols apply.
Contact prophylaxis doses are not covered in the sources opened.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: NICE advises parenteral antibiotics outside hospital for strongly suspected meningococcal disease, unless this delays transfer. Suspected meningitis is a medical emergency requiring urgent hospital transfer in all cases. A non-blanching rash with meningism or sepsis increases the likelihood of meningococcal disease. Antibiotics given in the community do not replace hospital assessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and call for transfer
actions: Treat suspected meningitis as a medical emergency; arrange urgent hospital transfer in all cases.
Do not delay transfer to give antibiotics.

clinicalManagement.title: Give parenteral antibiotics if indicated
actions: Adults and children 10–17 years: benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV or IM. Children 1–9 years: 600 mg. Children under 1 year: 300 mg.
Mild penicillin allergy: cefotaxime 2 g or ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM in adults.
Do not give if severe allergy to both ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin.

clinicalManagement.title: Handover
actions: Record the time and dose of antibiotics and pass it to the receiving emergency team.

regimens.indication: Suspected meningococcal disease or bacterial meningitis before hospital transfer
adjustments: Child 1–9 years: 600 mg; under 1 year: 300 mg.
No renal adjustment is given for a single dose in the source.
monitoring: Record time and dose; do not delay transfer.
contraindications: Severe allergy to benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone: do not give antibiotics outside hospital.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Strongly suspected meningococcal disease, or strongly suspected bacterial meningitis with likely significant transfer delay, unless it delays transfer.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Do not give antibiotics outside hospital
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Severe allergy to both ceftriaxone and benzylpenicillin.
Give antibiotics if transfer time is more than 1 hour, or if a non-blanching rash with meningism or sepsis is present and time permits.

teaching.scope: Community or pre-hospital recognition of suspected meningitis or meningococcal disease, immediate parenteral benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone when transfer is delayed, and urgent hospital transfer.
learningObjectives: Decide on pre-hospital antibiotics from transfer delay and rash.
pitfalls: Giving antibiotics to patients with severe allergy to both agents.
keyPoints: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g for adults and 10–17 years.
